items.body: From solo piano to orchestra, the music in this genre bears witness to life’s atrocities; it reflects the change of seasons; it seeks to console and uplift. Our top pick reintroduces us to a fallen friend, but new composers make an impact as well; one can never tell where the next great album will come from. Soon the leaves will begin to fall again, and then the snow, and then the rain, and then it will be summer. These composers bring us through life’s transitions, always looking forward to the next, teaching us the wisdom of cycles through the beauty of notes. Our cover image is taken from Jean-Michel Blais‘ mirador, covered below. Jóhann Jóhannsson has been gone nearly a decade now, and his absence is still felt. After a trickle of posthumous releases, we had grown resigned to the thought that we might never again hear new music from the composer. Meanwhile, Adam Wiltzie was working on unfinished pieces from a collaboration begun before the composer’s untimely death. We can think of no one better to tackle such a project. Adding to the sadness is the knowledge that Steve Albini helped with the production before he too was lost to the sands of time. Friendship Survival Guide is a tribute and a sonic keepsake; it’s a minor miracle that it exists at all. The first video is the beginning of a narrative thread; we can’t wait to see the rest! (Deutsche Grammophon, September 18). Also on Deutsche Grammophon, Icelandic composer Hildur Guðnadóttir reimagines her back catalogue with Robert Ames and the DSO Berlin. This Will Be Us breathes new life into these pieces and is preceded by non-album track “Floods” (October 23). The cover of Jean-Michel Blais‘ mirador looks like Max from Where the Wild Things Are sleeping off his evening; but it may also be a young man dreaming of adventure. The album is an ode to childhood imagination, bolstered by copious choirs and swirling strings (Arts & Crafts, September 25). Third Coast Percussion returns with Vernacular, the percussion ensemble’s 25th album. Jlin is now a full performing member, as heard on the opening single Premonition (Rockwell, October 23). Klara Lewis‘ Opening is already out, one of autumn’s early highlights. The album is awash in shades of blue, from art to music. After the abraded loops of “Ta Min Hand “, the set moves from form to abstraction, shifting like light through falling leaves (Editions Mego, September 4).   Justyna Jablonska‘s Unforeseen is a diverse set that addresses migration and memory through song, spoken word, voice and field recordings. The artist’s cello shines throughout the set, which culminates in a surprising rendition of “Shchedryk,” known to modern listeners as “Carol of the Bells” (Alumni Records Glasgow, September 4). Earlier this year, cellist Gaspar Claus impressed us with the score to French film Un Monde Violent. Now he returns with CELLS, which includes a contribution from Matt Elliott (Third Eye Foundation). The album is released September 25 on InFiné. Inspired by the work of visual artist James Turrell, Alyssa Weinberg‘s Pieces of Light, performed by cellist Gabriel Cabezas, plays with permutations of illumination. The album is preceded by the single ultraviolet (MASS MoCA, October 2).   Clerestory reflects its title, which refers to the windows in the upper section of walls, as found in churches. Jules Reidy uses this image to color the music, which highlights the interplay between shadow and light and whose single-track Side A is brought to light by JACK Quartet (Thrill Jockey, September 25). Twin Cities four-piece The Dust of Suns Ensemble offers Alyosha is a series of miniatures, inspired by Dostoyevsky, but with a playful aura. Released on September 1, early copies of the album are available on precious 10″ vinyl. We don’t receive many hurdy-gurdy albums, much less albums of hurdy-gurdy with violin and cello. Almost Starlight is one of these, recorded in a medieval church by Jem Finer (yes, that Jem Finer, from The Pogues!), John Matthias and Jay Auborn. The results are magical, mystical and ceremonial (Touch, September 4). Simon Goff‘s electronic chamber music is packed with violin and viola, with guest appearances by Anne Müller on cello. Interior Realms – vol. 1 is upbeat and life-affirming, on the surface a study of architecture but beneath this a treatise on the soul (Sonic Pieces, September 10). We can never tell where more eaze will head next, which is part of her appeal. On valley and structure, she heads for the heart of modern composition, even offering a score booklet. A host of guest starts decorates the set with new timbres and additional grace (Thrill Jockey, October 9).   Goldmund‘s In Each Moment is a gorgeous fall collection, inspired by the teachings of Buddhist nun Sister Dang Nghiem. The piano notes are as delicate as incense wafting to the sky, enhanced by some gentle ambient textures, producing a sense of perfect peace (Nettwerk, October 9). Chad Lawson‘s lowercase hush is as serene as can be, a prelude to winter. On held by evening, one can hear the almost hear the leaves as they start to fall (Decca, September 11). Jumping straight into that faraway season, Volodja Brodsky‘s piano-based Winterglare recalls the sun’s low angle in Estonia’s winter (We Are Busy Bodies, October 2). Piano player meets machine on The End is a Beginning, from the aptly named Postmodern Machine. The beats are warm and plentiful, but the ivories still hold court (Moderna, September 11). Some may recall that Björk’s first film role was in the feminist retelling of the Grimm tale The Juniper Tree. Forty years after it was written by Nietzchka Keene, the film receives a new score from Midori Hirano. The artist manages to tap into the tenderness and leans into the unsettling tension, with piano as the anchor and synthesizer as the encroachment (Viernulvier/Thrill Jockey, October 2). Ingfrid Breie Nyhus‘ Silkegul – Slåttepiano III is the third in a series of albums that investigate Norwegian folk traditions by means of the piano. As the nights grow longer, the notes will seem more and more fitting, like tales told around a fire (Lab, October 9).   Billed as a classical soul pianist, Alexis Ffrench releases the lush 24, two dozen pieces meant to comprise the soundtrack of a day. With tracks such as In Flight, crossover success is virtually guaranteed (Sony Classical, October 2). Pianist Sofi Paez releases Bodies of Water, inspired by Iceland’s diversity of natural beauty. Ocean is the first single (OPIA Community, September 25). Doubts and Loves Like a Mole is the new EP from pianist Nathan Schubert, preceded by the peaceful, brass-inflected single Schillerpromenade (Bigo & Twigeitti, October 2). Brandon Hopkins follows Three Commutes with Piano Etudes, Book I, six works of tender wisdom (September 25). On the cover of conditions for observing light, pianist Cephas Azariah seems to have been shot through with a sunbeam. The metaphor applies to the composer’s work, which also touches on ambient and electronic territory, while searching fro radiance in all of its forms (Anjunachill, September 3). With radiant contributions from Clarice Jensen and Spencer Zahn, Sova (Sophia Vastek) can do no wrong. As one might expect from the title, early single “Heavy Shit” is an exercise in darkness, but the album Alight! is a study of contrasts, anchored by Sova’s exquisite keys (Hout, September 4). Double bass and electronics merge on Fragments, an album long in the making; Fragment I debuted in 2025. By blending genres, ZKHR hopes to appeal to multiple audiences (September 19).   Dobrinka Tabakova has been accumulating the pieces of Stone Trail for nearly a quarter-century; now they are gathered in one place. The album is graced with numerous collaborators, and is one of our furthest-out releases, dropping November 13 on NMC. The first half of Episodic Memory includes a murder ballad, but the second is a vibrant instrumental suite that comments on the experience of trauma. Exceptet and Bendon Randall-Myers handle both with aplomb (cmntx, October 9). Daniella Ljungsberg splits Other Plans between vocal and instrumental pieces, but when she sings, she does so with reverence, honoring the Baroque nature of these tender Nordic folk tales (ORTHODOX, October 2). Alfredo Ovalles and Black Page Orchestra present The Art of Parties on September 18, preceded by the inviting single Dance! (PARMA). Richard Allen

items.body: DiN has built an extensive catalogue through precisely these kinds of creative connections, and Juxtapositions stands as a particularly strong example of what can emerge when experienced artists remain genuinely open to one another. There is considerable craft here. Its sophistication lies in the natural way its many elements coexist and transform. The realization of a conversation that required time to develop Juxtapositions (DiN97) by Boddy | Scanner   Collaboration can be a particularly revealing form of musical exchange. When two artists with long-established identities enter the same creative space, the result can either reinforce familiar strengths or uncover previously unexplored territory. On Juxtapositions, Ian Boddy and Scanner, the recording identity of Robin Rimbaud, accomplish the latter with remarkable assurance. Both are legendary figures within the broad landscape of electronic music, yet they approach sound from distinctly different perspectives. That contrast becomes the central strength of this nine-track collaboration. Released on Boddy‘s long-running DiN imprint, Juxtapositions brings together two musicians whose individual careers have been defined by curiosity, exploration, and an ability to continually expand their respective vocabularies. Scanner has previously appeared on DiN through his solo releases An Ascent and The Homeland of Electricity, while his work alongside Boddy at Manchester’s Subliminal Impulse festival ​in 2022 offered an earlier indication of what their musical connection might produce. Four years later, Juxtapositions feels less like a casual meeting of established artists and more like the realization of a conversation that required time to develop.   Fragments, environmental recordings, and elusive electronic details :: The album’s title is particularly appropriate. Boddy and Rimbaud‘s approaches remain identifiable, but neither musician simply occupies a separate half of the sound field. Instead, their contrasting methods continually intersect and reshape one another. Cycling electronic patterns emerge and gradually lose their boundaries within more diffuse textures. Carefully articulated sequences create a sense of forward movement before dissolving into reverberant spaces filled with fragments, environmental recordings, and elusive electronic details. The opening “Exclusion Zone” immediately establishes this sense of unstable balance. Repetition and atmosphere coexist without either becoming dominant, creating a piece that seems simultaneously structured and unsettled. The duo understands the expressive potential of restraint. Ideas are allowed to develop gradually, and changes in texture or emphasis often arrive so naturally that the listener may only recognize the transformation after it has already occurred. “A Passing Trace” continues this approach with an appropriately elusive quality, while “Voltage in Bloom” introduces a more energized sense of motion. Throughout the album, Boddy‘s sensitivity to melodic and sequential development provides an important sense of internal architecture, while Scanner‘s interventions introduce ambiguity, disruption, and a fascination with the physical and accidental characteristics of sound. The combination is particularly effective because neither artist appears interested in forcing a stylistic compromise. “Sotto Voce” explores quieter territory, allowing subtle shifts in tone and atmosphere to carry much of the composition’s emotional weight. This is followed by “Intersignals,” where fragments of communication and electronic activity become part of the musical environment. Scanner‘s recognizable use of radio transmissions and found audio is particularly effective throughout Juxtapositions. These elements never feel like decorative references or conceptual interruptions. Instead, they introduce a human presence that is distant, fragmented, and often impossible to fully understand. Source material and electronic processing become increasingly difficult to locate :: That tension between familiarity and abstraction becomes increasingly important as the album progresses. Field recordings from old houses and reverberant cellars suggest physical spaces without reducing them to easily identifiable locations. They become acoustic environments within the compositions, their resonances and imperfections blending with synthesized sound until distinctions between source material and electronic processing become increasingly difficult to locate. “A Room of Hammers” is among the album’s most evocative titles and its slightly extended duration allows the duo to explore a particularly rich interplay between texture, resonance, and implied physicality. Sounds seem to occupy depth rather than simply appearing across the stereo field. There is a strong sense of entering spaces within the music, each one containing its own acoustic characteristics and hidden activity. The final third of the album demonstrates how successfully Boddy and Scanner have established a shared language. “Shared Frequencies” is perhaps the most fitting title in this respect, suggesting not merely collaboration but communication through common ground discovered in the process of making the music. “Mnemonic Patterns” returns to the album’s interest in repetition and evolving structures, while “A Fleeting Glimpse” brings Juxtapositions to a close without imposing a conventional sense of resolution. This album’s most compelling moments are often found in the details: a pattern that changes almost imperceptibly, a distant tone entering and disappearing, a reverberation suggesting an unexpected depth, or a texture gradually assuming a different character. Two distinctive musical voices discover new possibilities :: What makes Juxtapositions especially successful is that it avoids the temptation to present collaboration as a competition between recognizable styles. Boddy and Rimbaud bring their histories and individual sensibilities into the project, but the resulting music belongs to neither artist alone. Their differences become productive points of tension, generating compositions that move between hypnotic repetition, abstract sound design, emotional resonance, and carefully constructed electronic space. DiN has built an extensive catalogue through precisely these kinds of creative connections, and Juxtapositions stands as a particularly strong example of what can emerge when experienced artists remain genuinely open to one another. There is considerable craft here. Its sophistication lies in the natural way its many elements coexist and transform. For listeners familiar with either artist, Juxtapositions offers the pleasure of hearing two distinctive musical voices discover new possibilities through their interaction. For those encountering their work for the first time, it is an absorbing entry point into the creative worlds of both Boddy and Scanner. More importantly, it stands on its own as a deeply considered and beautifully constructed electronic work, one whose subtle movement and hidden detail encourage repeated listening. Juxtapositions is an album about the productive possibilities of difference. Ian Boddy and Robin Rimbaud do not erase the distance between their individual sound worlds. They explore it. Within that space between their approaches, they have created something rich, patient, mysterious, and quietly compelling. Juxtapositions is available on DiN. items.body: Across Another World, Artificial Island keep things measured and textural, allowing minute sounds, gentle rhythms and shifting layers to carry much of the album’s character. A calm range of ambient-electronic soundscapes Another World by Artificial Island   London-based duo Artificial Island, lifelong friends Gareth Williams and Ian Prytherch, announce their debut album, Another World, bringing together some of their strongest material from previous releases alongside three new tracks: “Spirit,” “A Different Sun,” and “Departure.” It also includes their most widely recognized track, “Emerge,” a delicate blend of softened synth tones and lullaby-like melodies. All material has been remastered by Guy Davie at Electric Mastering in London, whose credits include Jon Hopkins, Marconi Union and Four Tet. Between cascading ambient-techno archways and ethereal waves of light, Another World generates carefully focused momentum. Traversing Another World, Artificial Island gradually unfolds a calm range of ambient-electronic soundscapes, with each track given room to develop through subtle shifts in texture and tone. “After Dark” is built around a floating atmosphere, soft electronic tones and light glitches that drift in and out of focus. “A Different Sun” introduces neo-classical elements, gently moving through cinematic textures and restrained melodic passages, while “Departure” focuses on microscopic details, weaving soft blips and bleeps aro​und low-flying beat pulses and a steady, understated rhythmic strain. As the album moves towards its closing tracks, “Lodestar” returns to spacious, celestial textures, balancing subtle movement with a sense of stillness. Closing piece “Lumen” takes a more distant approach, built from isolated ambient tones, soft electronic whirs and fragments that seem to hover just beyond reach. Across Another World, Artificial Island keep things measured and textural, allowing minute sounds, gentle rhythms and shifting layers to carry much of the album’s character. Built around atmospheric electronics, ambient textures and carefully layered detail, Another World should appeal to fans of Boards of Canada, Marconi Union and Carbon Based Lifeforms. The artwork was designed by Chris Bigg, who spent three decades at 4AD’s legendary v23 design studio alongside Vaughan Oliver, creating artwork for Pixies, Cocteau Twins, Dead Can Dance, The Breeders, and David Sylvian. Bigg has remained David Sylvian’s long-time design collaborator ever since. Another World is self-released on October 2, 2026, available across streaming platforms as well as CD and a limited-edition 2x180g white-vinyl pressing. items.body: Review by maxsmusic — A compilation of a few composers. If compared to other music of the era, this one is fresh and holds up today. This is synthetic music realized on synths so people generally like it or hate it. The synthesizer is a marvelous invention and it can generate wave forms based on parameters put into the patch. When it comes close to acoustic sound waves, it has the most warmth and soul. The problem is that the overtones in synthetic sound production will never come close to the complex overtones of an acoustic instrument. However, these musicians know how to manipulate sound and they give it a funkiness and beat that makes it very enjoyable.

items.body: Madra Salach‘s “The Man Who Seeks Pleasure (Live from London)” was recorded on the last night of the band’s sold-out debut headline tour, at The Dome in Tufnell Park in March, and arrived on Island Records on 26 June. The song first appeared on the Dublin band’s debut EP, It’s a Hell of an Age, released in January, which reached number three on the Irish Albums Chart, broke into the UK’s Official Independent Albums Chart top ten and earned the band live sessions for BBC 6 Music’s Steve Lamacq and Radio 1’s New Music Fix. Paul Banks built the song around indulgence undercut by consequence, pleasure and pain framed as two names for the same want, setting the scene early with the image “lick the sugar off the cane.” The London version stretches that tension out with the full band: Jack Martin and Adam Cullen‘s guitar and mandolin lines wind around each other, Maxime Arnold‘s harmonium deepens the drone underneath, and Dara Duffy and Jack Lawlor push the song harder on drums and bass than the EP cut allows. Banks has said the recording comes from “the last show on our debut headline tour,” and that the band wanted a version built around the full arrangement rather than the more minimal EP take. The band follow the release with a run of summer festival dates including Electric Picnic and Green Man, before returning to headline UK and Irish venues in October. items.body: Fields of the Nephilim, the English gothic rock band from Stevenage, Hertfordshire, released “The Nephilim” on 5 September 1988 through Situation Two, an imprint of Beggars Banquet. The album turns 38 this year. It was the band’s second studio album, it followed “Dawnrazor” from 1987, and it entered the UK album chart at number 12. The record was made in a former courthouse. Sessions took place at The Justice Room in the Somerset countryside, a building where prisoners sentenced to death had been hanged on site. Bassist Tony Pettitt described the setting in a 2013 PopMatters retrospective on the album’s 25th year: “The place had a really cool vibe”. Mixing moved to Genetic Studios and the master was cut at Tape One. Sources differ on the production credit: the Situation Two sleeve lists Bill Buchanan as producer with the band credited in association, while Wikipedia gives the band itself. Brad Davis recorded the sessions, Timm Baldwin mixed, and Ian Gillespie handled pre-mastering. The line-up was Carl McCoy on vocals, Pettitt on bass, Peter Yates and Paul Wright on guitars, and Alexander “Nod” Wright on drums. ‘The Nephilim’ formats, tracklist and credits Situation Two issued the album in the UK as a gatefold LP with printed lyrics to “The Watchman” and “Last Exit for the Lost”, and on CD and cassette. Rebel Rec. handled the German pressing through SPV, and Beggars Banquet released it in the United States with RCA. The vinyl runs eight tracks: “Endemoniada”, “The Watchman”, “Phobia”, “Moonchild”, “Chord of Souls”, “Celebrate”, “Love Under Will” and “Last Exit for the Lost”. The CD adds a ninth, “Shiva”, which had been the B-side of the “Moonchild” single. Chris Bigg designed the sleeve, Simon Larbalestier shot the outer photography, Julian Calverley the inner gatefold, and Lynn S supplied the lyric calligraphy. “Moonchild” reached number 28 in the UK singles chart, well above the number 75 the band had managed a year earlier with “Blue Water”. Several titles point outward: “Moonchild” shares its name with a novel by Aleister Crowley, “Love Under Will” takes a phrase from his Book of the Law, and the lyrics to “The Watchman” and “Last Exit for the Lost” reference H. P. Lovecraft’s Cthulhu. The opening track, “Endemoniada”, carries a sample of Ron Perlman growling “Penitenziagite!” as the hunchback Salvatore in the 1986 film “The Name of the Rose”. Beggars Archive returned to the album on 20 October 2023 with a double-LP reissue pressed on golden brown vinyl and expanded with three bonus tracks. About Fields of the Nephilim Carl McCoy, Tony Pettitt, Paul Wright, Alexander “Nod” Wright and saxophonist Gary Wisker formed Fields of the Nephilim in Stevenage, Hertfordshire, in 1984. The name refers both to the biblical race of angel-human hybrids and to the magnetic fields around the Earth. Peter Yates joined on guitar in 1985, the year the band put out its debut 12″ EP “Burning the Fields” on its own Tower Release label. Jungle Records picked the record up and put the band back in the studio for the “Returning to Gehenna” EP. Situation Two signed them in 1986 and issued the singles “Power” and “Preacher Man”. The first album, “Dawnrazor”, topped the UK indie chart in 1987, and “Blue Water” became their first entry on the UK singles chart. “The Nephilim” followed in 1988. “Psychonaut” arrived in May 1989 and peaked at number 35, its ten-minute running time pointing toward the more layered approach of “Elizium” in 1990. For that album the band moved up to the Beggars Banquet imprint and worked with Andy Jackson, an engineer for Pink Floyd and David Gilmour, in place of Bill Buchanan. Its lead single “For Her Light” clipped the UK top 40 in its first week, and a remixed “Sumerland (Dreamed)” reached number 37 that November. The band played its last shows of that era in 1991, a two-day Festival of Fire at the Town & Country Club in London, documented on the live album “Earth Inferno” and the video “Visionary Heads”. McCoy left the same year. The remaining members recruited singer Andy Delaney and continued as Rubicon, releasing “What Starts, Ends” in 1992 and “Room 101” in 1995. McCoy started Nefilim, whose album “Zoon” was held back by label disagreements until 1996. McCoy and Pettitt announced a return at a press conference during the Zillo Festival in Germany on 15 August 1998. The single “One More Nightmare (Trees Come Down)” came out on Jungle Records in May 2000, reworking two songs from “Burning the Fields”, and the band played Woodstage, Eurorock, Roskilde and M’era Luna that summer. Jungle issued “Fallen” in 2002 with licensees including Metropolis Records and SPV; the band disowned it, and only one of its songs has been played live. McCoy’s fourth full-length under the Fields of the Nephilim name, “Mourning Sun”, appeared in 2005 with a cover of Zager and Evans’ “In the Year 2525” as a bonus track on the first 5,000 copies. A new line-up played the London Astoria in May 2007, the first Fields of the Nephilim show in seven years, and headlined M’era Luna in 2008 in front of a crowd of more than 23,000. Recordings from two Shepherd’s Bush Empire nights became “Ceromonies (Ad Mortem Ad Vitam)”, released on McCoy’s Sacred Symphony label on 16 April 2012. Beggars Archive collected the first three studio albums, “Earth Inferno” and a singles-and-remixes disc in a five-album box in November 2013. McCoy said in July 2014 that the band was back in the studio; “Earthbound” and “Prophecy” were played live that December, and “Prophecy” was issued as a single on 17 March 2016, produced, engineered and mixed by McCoy and mastered by Maor Appelbaum. Guitarist Tom Edwards, who played with the band between 2008 and 2016, died of heart failure in January 2017 while touring the United States with Adam Ant, reported at the time in Fields of the Nephilim / Adam Ant guitarist Tom Edwards dies aged 41. Beggars Archive has kept the back catalogue moving since then, with the expanded “The Nephilim” in October 2023, a 30th anniversary red vinyl “Elizium” on 5 April 2024, and a remastered “Dawnrazor” on 12 December 2025. The current line-up is McCoy on vocals, Pettitt on bass and Gavin King and Adam Leach on guitars. Thirty-eight years on, “The Nephilim” still sits at the centre of that catalogue, between the indie-chart-topping “Dawnrazor” and the wider reach of “Elizium”.

items.body: Skinny Puppy released their second studio album, “Mind: The Perpetual Intercourse,” through Nettwerk on 5 September 1986. The Vancouver industrial band’s sophomore record turns 40 this year. It is the album that introduced keyboardist Dwayne Goettel to the lineup and pushed the group’s sound away from its early synth-pop leanings toward a heavier, sample-driven style. Dave Ogilvie and cEvin Key produced, engineered and mixed the album, which was released on vinyl and cassette through Nettwerk in Canada and the US and through Play It Again Sam in Europe; Capitol Records-EMI handled Canadian distribution, a deal that expanded the record’s retail reach from roughly 200 to 1,700 stores across the country. The cover, a photograph by frequent collaborator Steven R. Gilmore taken from a pornographic film he saw on a hotel television in New York City, later won Best Album Art at the 1987 CASBY Awards and landed the record on one of Tipper Gore’s Parents Music Resource Center lists. A 1988 CD reissue on Capitol Records added four bonus tracks, including the single “Chainsaw,” to the original nine-song lineup. The lead single, “Dig It,” received regular MTV airplay and a Billboard recommendation, and “Stairs and Flowers” followed as a second single; Skinny Puppy toured North America and Europe with Severed Heads to support the release. “Mind: The Perpetual Intercourse” streams on Bandcamp and is also available on Spotify. Mind: The Perpetual Intercourse by Skinny Puppy About Skinny Puppy Skinny Puppy started in Vancouver, Canada, in 1982 as a side project for drummer cEvin Key (born Kevin Crompton), who was also playing in the new wave band Images in Vogue. Key brought in vocalist Nivek Ogre (Kevin Ogilvie), and the two adopted stage names to tell the two Kevins apart. The pair self-released the “Back & Forth” EP in 1983 and signed to the Vancouver label Nettwerk that same year. A second EP, “Remission,” followed in December 1984, and the debut album, “Bites,” arrived in 1985 with Bill Leeb, performing as Wilhelm Schroeder, on bass synth and backing vocals. Leeb left in 1986 to start Front Line Assembly, and Key hired keyboardist Dwayne Goettel to replace him. Goettel, a classically trained pianist with a background in samplers and the Ensoniq Mirage, had met Key the year before, when his band Water opened for Skinny Puppy. He made his first appearance on record on “Mind: The Perpetual Intercourse,” released 5 September 1986. Key later called Goettel “the master of sampling.” Skinny Puppy went on to release “Cleanse Fold and Manipulate” (1987), “VIVIsectVI” (1988), “Rabies” (1989, featuring Ministry’s Al Jourgensen), “Too Dark Park” (1990) and “Last Rights” (1992), their final album for Nettwerk. In 1993 the band signed to Rick Rubin’s American Recordings and moved to Los Angeles to record “The Process.” Ogre left the band in June 1995, and Goettel died two months later, on 23 August 1995, at the age of 31. Key and producer Dave “Rave” Ogilvie completed “The Process,” releasing it in 1996 in Goettel’s memory. Skinny Puppy reunited for a one-off show in Dresden, Germany, in 2000 and became a full-time act again in 2003 with producer Mark Walk, releasing “The Greater Wrong of the Right” (2004), “Mythmaker” (2007), “HanDover” (2011) and “Weapon” (2013). “Mind: The Perpetual Intercourse” turns 40 in 2026 as the first Skinny Puppy album to feature Goettel, who remained with the band until his death in 1995.

items.body: The Romanian collective Nam-Khar has been active since 2009, releasing numerous albums and collaborations over the years. In recent years, much of their work has appeared on labels such as Zazen Sounds, Winter-Light, and, more recently, Cyclic Law. With this new release, Nam-Khar explores a concept centered on alchemy, specifically the transformation of the self; the connection to—and inspiration drawn from—psychoanalytic pioneers such as Freud and Jung is therefore evident. It is no coincidence that the album comprises seven tracks, a number of symbolic significance in alchemy. Here, Nam-Khar gives free rein to their creativity. While the music remains rooted in the Ritual genre, it is clearly much more than that. It incorporates strong Dark-Ambient elements alongside Industrial sounds and a pronounced Cinematic influence, manifesting itself primarily in deep, astral passages. Add a healthy dose of experimentation to the mix, and you get a sense of the highly diverse “Antimon”, where magical analogue sounds, acoustic instruments, and field recordings converge. The album oscillates between mysterious, dreamlike passages and others that are menacing and ominous. With “Antimon”, Nam-Khar once again delivers a compelling release that is sure to captivate a wider audience interested in the aforementioned genres. (Rating:8). Listen to “Melanosis”: Melanosis by Nam-Khar About Nam-Khar Nam-Khar is a ritual ambient project centered on Romanian musician Konchog Gyaltsen, active since 2009. The project debuted with “A Hallowed Ground Within” the same year, and its catalog mixes ritual and dark ambient with industrial and cinematic elements, built from ethnic instrumentation, analog synthesis and field recordings. Nam-Khar released “Secret Essence / Sangwa Dupa” (CD, Winter-Light) in 2018 and “Sur Chöd” (Winter-Light) in 2020, followed by “Dok-Pa” (Zazen Sounds) in 2022, a sequence Cyclic Law describes as the project’s “Tibetan Trilogy”. The same year brought “Nag-Hammadi” (Winter-Light), a collaboration with Vortex. Nam-Khar has also recorded with Alone in the Hollow Garden and Sielwolf, releasing “The Sarajevo Spiral” with Vortex and “Antariksha” as Alone In The Hollow Garden & Nam-Khar, both in 2024. With “Antimon”, released July 20, 2026 on Zazen Sounds and Cyclic Law, Nam-Khar returns after “The Sarajevo Spiral” with a seven-track album built around an alchemical concept.

items.body: Some artists move between genres as tourists, collecting a new set of surfaces with every release. Kontravoid moves differently. Across skeletal coldwave, heavy EBM, freestyle-informed electro, industrial club music, and dark pop, Cameron Findlay has maintained a character that can be recognized within seconds: disciplined drums, bass that seems to alter the air pressure, synthesizers suspended between metallic seduction and industrial alarm, and an abrasive baritone that sounds transmitted from a sealed room. That consistency amid constant movement has made Kontravoid one of the most important acts in the international darkwave and EBM scene. The Canadian-born, Los Angeles-based musician, drummer, and producer has announced a new full-length album, Sound of the Void, due October 2, 2026, through Toronto’s Artoffact Records. It will be his second album for Artoffact, coming more than two years after his previous release, Detachment, which came out on March 1, 2024. The announcement includes the new single “Without,” joining January’s “Mortal” as the second track available ahead of the album. The space between albums has hardly been empty. Findlay carried Detachment through Europe and North America, appearing at Wave-Gotik-Treffen and playing dates alongside Buzz Kull and Cold Cave. In December 2024, Losing Game Remixes returned to his collaboration with Nuovo Testamento vocalist Chelsey Crowley, while Crowley’s band Nuovo Testamento, Normal Bias, Auragraph, and Tassel each pulled the song into a different corner of the club. Findlay also continued his parallel life as a remixer, recasting Ekko the Strange’s “Reanimate,” Modern English’s “Not My Leader,” Mareux’s “The Perfect Girl,” Buzz Kull’s “In the Cut,” and Raudiver’s “No Sun Rising.” The list stretches from foundational British post-punk to contemporary dark pop, but each rework retains his familiar low-end physicality and severe rhythmic control. That versatility reaches back beyond the mask. Before launching Kontravoid in 2012, Findlay co-founded the Toronto synthpop group Parallels and played drums with Crystal Castles and TR/ST. Kontravoid gave those experiences a single, durable identity, allowing him to change tempo, density, and genre without losing the tension at the center of his music. Findlay’s forthcoming album, Sound of the Void, promises to seamlessly blend coldwave textures with thunderous EBM basslines and pulsating electro rhythms, elevating the body-focused electronic style that has characterized Kontravoid’s recent releases. Yet, “Without” hints that the album will transcend mere repetition of Detachment. The new single “Without” opens on a throbbing bass synthesizer, an alarm-like synthwave figure, and drums pressing forward in precise, heavy strokes. Findlay delivers clipped poetic lines through a harsh vocal treatment as warped synthesizers bend around him. When the verse breaks apart, his voice gives way to a flood of effects surrounding a series of shouts. Dark pads, driving electro rhythms, and lush basslines gather into a cold, nearly solid wall of sound, pulling the track toward something disembodied and otherworldly. The song sits outside any single darkwave, EBM, or coldwave designation, though every pressure point bears Kontravoid’s signature. It is a different kind of Kontravoid track, and a clear example of Findlay operating at the top of his game: widening the project’s vocabulary while keeping its identity intact. Listen to “Without” below and pre-order Sound of the Void here. Sound of the Void by Kontravoid Sound of the Void was produced by Findlay and mixed and mastered by Ewan A. Kay. Dylan Frankland contributed live drums to “Without” and closing track “Phantom,” with Daryl Dee handling the live-drum engineering. Jean Lorenzo designed the cover, while Los Angeles photographer Corinne Schiavone, also known as Perpetual Mobile, supplied the original insert photograph. The ten-track album will be available digitally, on CD, and on clear vinyl. A limited black-vinyl test pressing with white labels is also available. The digital edition and CD arrive October 2, while the first vinyl pressing is expected to ship around November 20. Digital preorders include immediate downloads of “Without” and “Mortal.” The album received funding support from FACTOR, the Government of Canada, and Canadian private radio broadcasters. Sound of the Void Tracklist Sound of the Void Without Mortal Subject Chances Dimension Forever Abandon Returning Phantom The album announcement precedes Kontravoid’s 27-date North American co-headlining tour with Australian electronic artist Buzz Kull. The run begins September 10 at Elysium in Austin and concludes October 24 at the SUBSTANCE festival in Los Angeles. The October 2 album release falls on the tour’s Kansas City stop. Spike Hellis and Normal Bias will join the bill in Spokane, Vancouver, Seattle, Portland, and Sacramento. Tickets and further information are available through Kontravoid’s official website. items.body: We are extremely excited about the Experimental segment of our Fall Music Preview, as it contains all manner of treasures! This fall’s releases include an album that concentrates on the metallic aspects of percussion and other works inspired by biomes, nest building and Haruki Murakami’s IQ84. The youngest performers are in the single digits, while the oldest is an octogenarian. With such a wide variety here on display, there’s something for everyone to enjoy. So set aside all expectations, put those earbuds in and prepare to be dazzled! Our cover image is a lovely collage designed by Sonnenzimmer for Katherine Young‘s BIOMES, covered below. Electroacoustic Lea Bertucci and Michael Beharie may be vying for attention with Sarah Davachi come year’s end, as Bow and Arrow walks through similar glens. Their sound, billed as “electroacoustic spectral folk,” puts one in mind of autumn and its mysterious natural timbres (NNA Tapes, October 23). Weston Olenki and TAK ensemble‘s when the great fires were lit on the other side of the ocean is one of the season’s most distinct recordings, inspired by the writings of W.G. Sebald on electricity and including field recordings from Tesla’s first power plant. The limited edition includes both the score and a lecture packet (Sweet Wreath, September 30). Hallow Ground offers John McCowen‘s Pressure Chords feat. Lucy Railton, Weston Olencki, an album that could just as easily landed in our Drone department. With contrabass clarinet, cello and trombone, the trio stretches tones taffy-thin before rebuilding them layer by layer (September 18). After this comes Jordan Sand‘s Baby Ghost, whose tendrils of falsetto voice are mingled with passages of bowed double bass, producing an otherworldly effect (October 2).   Free improvisation meets metal and drone on Mats Erlandsson & Gus Loxbo‘s Minnets Långa Kedjor (XKatedral, September 18), a moody album with narration from Maria W Horn. At times, the work invokes Swans, which makes sense as Michael Gira offers guest narration on Horn’s own album, Melting Pillars of Snow, out October 2 on the same label. Buy them both to experience the depths of a dark autumn.   Misanthropic Agenda‘s first releases of the season are out today. Vincent Grimaldi‘s Amorcie De Champ is crinkly and dark, a collage of field recordings, turntables and tapes, while the troublingly named Perverts in White Shirts offers “cringe pop” on the 28-track CULTrully appropriate songs and revisited memories (September 4). The creaks, rustles and cracks of Liths (Sarah Hennies, Willie B. and Keir Neuringer) make Ascending the Depths a perfect album for fall, when the shadows creep across the forest floor and strange creatures come out to play (Dinzu Artefacts, September 25).   Mark Peter Wright offers pure North Yorkshire field recordings on Field Crafting, interacting with his environment in a way that honors his surroundings while bringing them to life (Flaming Pines, October 8). Icelandic field recordings decorate the background of Marja Ahti & John McCowen‘s Errands, which fills in the spaces with recorder and clarinet (Black Truffle, September 25). Mixing field recordings with electro-acoustic elements, Crys Cole presents Testing the Waters, a single-track album whose rivers run deep (Persistence of Sound, October 9). Midway between minimalism and drone lies Roel Meelkop‘s Antithesis, a set sounds that relate to each other in interlocking ways (Crónica, September 8). CZN (copper, zinc and nickel) combines the work of percussionist-sculptor João Pais Filipe, composer-drummer Valentina Magaletti, and producer Leon Marks. The concentration on gongs, cymbals and other metal objects earns the trio its moniker, hearkening back to the work of mHz. Parallel Commutator is out October 16 on Oath.   Katherine Young‘s BIOMES is breathy and intense, initially inspired by lichen before expanding into wetlands, oyster reefs and more. Joining the artist: Olivia Block, Ben LaMar Gay, Brian Chase, Tim Daisy, and Yarn/Wire, who help to make the album a three-dimensional experience (Chaikin, September 18). We’re loving the sheets of rain in “Thunder Covered Brush,” the opening track of M. Sage‘s Brush Flier. The artist draws from multiple genres on this album, including ambient, folk and electronic, keeping the dynamic contrast high (RVNG Intl., September 25). ICMC: Best of the Listening Rooms is an electro-acoustic extravaganza, drawing from the 50th anniversary of the International Computer Music Conference. Featuring music from around the world, the compilation is as much a treat for the mind as it is the ears (Ravello, September 18). Yanick Soland is Walking on Rubber Eggshells. The set is a potpourri of sounds: flute, violin, zither, bowed koto and voice. Originally part of a solo exhibition, it displays the “come hither” sound that in person must have drawn people into the room (Futura Resistenza, September 28). Kaoru Watanabe‘s The Arch draws the listener deep into Japanese musical heritage, as the composer plays multiple instruments, including shinobue, ryuteki, hichiriki, taiko, atarigane, suzu, ame uchiwa, and koto, along with some instruments associated with the West. The songs tell stories, teach lessons, and entertain (New Amsterdam, September 18). Using “rage as a creative process,” Marina Herlop presents Dja Dja, which contains multiple nooks and crannies, featuring gamelan, voice and unconventional rhythms, and ultimately comes across as positive. There’s even a t-shirt bundle (October 9).   Jazz and Improvisation 577 Records always has its act together when it comes to pre-orders, which is why they get the lead-off spot. But this season, their first release is a true outlier. Released through the Positive Elevation imprint, the self-titled MY FACE IS DANCING is a family affair ~ specifically, the family of Federico Ughi, who records with his three sons. There’s hip-hop here alongside the jazz, and even some slam poetry: a photo album in sonic form (September 4). Two weeks later, Rafael Zaldivar | McBride | Mela release the languid Meeting in New York, Volume One, which was just recorded this past April (September 18). Savant Fleur follows with the raucous Hocketus, which indulges in dissonance, atonalism and noise, mangling the strings of the cello and violin (September 25). Then the attention turns to the solo work of Cuban musician Francesco Mela, playing multiple instruments on Carnavale De Oriente (October 9). (Mela also has an album out this fall with Nicki Adams and Michael Eaton; Arrival is released on J-Man Records September 10, preceded by the title track.) AIRLFT‘s Spatial Recognition began as a monthly meeting, turned into a community and has now become an album (October 16). We’ll Let You Know When We Find Out, declare Sonelius Smith and Adam Kahan, mixing originals with standards by Monk, Beethoven and Gershwin (October 23). Gon Muruaga leads an international trio on Lines in the Sky, an extremely active recording overflowing with happy notes (October 28). On November 11 we’ll hear FRAGMENTS, from bassist and bandleader Bishu Chattopadhyay, followed a day later by Pat Thomas‘ playful Of all people…, preceded by the highly unusual and engaging “OOPS” (November 12).   Not to be outdone, Endectomorph Music has announced nine fall albums, taking us all the way through December. The fun begins with Christian Li‘s Broken Neon Sign, a mix of instrumental and vocal, improvised and composed (September 4). Then the attention turns to alto saxophonist Kevin Sun for I and II, which includes a cover of “Laura Palmer’s Theme” (September 25). Sunhyun Yoo‘s PLAiDE is filled with sax and decorated with synth and Moog (October 2). Next is the sextet Sundate on October 9, followed by pianist Dabin Ryu and friends on Discomfort. (November 6). Be sure to save room for Matei Predescu‘s Basmeon November 20, Joechen Rueckert’s New Quartet on How to Survive a Beheading (November 20) and Ocelot‘s II on December 4: a generous slate! The Travel Agency Is On Fire is one of the wildest releases of the season. The four-disc box set is a tribute to William S. Burroughs, billed as Anne Waldman, Thurston Moore, James Ilgenfritz, Anagram Ensemble but involving many other guest stars, from Bill Laswell to Tortoise. Fans of spoken word poetry and improv should order on the spot (Infrequent Seams, September 25).   Viola artist Jessica Pavone plays solo on half of …Is In the Air and collaborates on the other half, the best of both worlds (Relative Pitch/Weird Cry, October 16). Given the rather bland title Four Pieces for Viola and Sampler, one might expect the album to be a staid affair; quite the contrary. AJ Nilles & Tom Schneider are often raucous and always wild; you can’t judge an album by the title! (Macro, October 9). Avant cellist Topo Lyo offers quiet scenes from tokyo, embracing bass-like notes with tape loops while constructing humble tributes to nature (Faitiche, November 6). Out of Your Head Records launches autumn with The Realist, showcasing the work of cellist Janel Leppin (September 11). Then it will be time for Mali Obomsawin, the bassist and vocalist leading a nonet on the diverse Automatic (October 16). Next on the docket is acoustic bassist Stephan Crump, who leads a quartet on Passerine, inspired by the work of birds building their nests (October 23). Ambiances Magnétiques has two releases slated for September 25. Érick d’Orion‘s Mes fantômes is thick in some places, thin in others, so that one can hear the phantom threads. Super Scintillant‘s Tarot is jazzier, reflecting the interplay between bass clarinet and modular synthesizer, thanks to Mélanie Bourassa and Nicolas Bernier. Earshift is prepping two releases for September. Awakening is a collection of Armenian music, brought to life by the ensemble Visions of Nar (September 18), while trumpeter Tom Avgenicos leads a quartet on I’ll Go Where You Go as Delay 45, with an emphasis on dynamic contrast (September 25). A large part of Adam Rudolph‘s ensemble is from Türkiye, which results in some fascinating timbres of ney, cuika, waterphone and darbuka. Toys and found objects are also included. Invisible Threads is out on Northern Spy, September 18. Payton MacDonald leads marimba and percussion duos on Transients Vol. 1, 2, & 3, pairing with Susie Ibarra, Billy Martin and Nava Dunkelman (Infrequent Seams, September 4). Baritone saxophonist Tamar Osborn is set to release Varier: Berlin, the first of two albums to be recorded with separate ensembles. (Varier: London will follow next year.) The album is a celebration of the sights and sounds of the city, suffused with an underlying grief and eventual healing as the artist mourns the death of her father (October 2). Duologues 7: Distillation is the latest release from the saxophone and piano duo of Ivo Perelman and Matthew Shipp. Squidco is promising to release a new collaboration every year “in perpetuum” (October 2).   Blair / Huber‘s ECLIPSE is a thoughtful work for saxophone and guitar, the first of an extensive fall slate for LEITER; the rest is under wraps for now (October 16). Liba Villavecchia and Vasco Trilla (sax and drums) make a joyful noise on Serrat, with two side-long jams and album art that reflects the angular sound (defkaz, September 1). Sax and drums duo Nicole McCabe and Savannah Harris offer the warm and friendly All Together Now, prefaced by the single Lonely People, which makes them seem anything but (Sudden Quarterly, September 18). Likely the oldest performer in this article, trumpeter Wadada Leo Smith is still going strong at age 84. Constellations and Hemispheres finds the musician voyaging into inner and outer space with the help of four ensembles, a testament to his versatility (Burning Ambulance, September 25). Also released on Burning Ambulance, trumpeter Michael Sarian presents In This Desert, anchored by the three-part title track, redolent of heat shimmer and wide open spaces (September 25).   Images on loan is the first taste of Yuma Koda‘s enveloping Amid Kinos, which includes appearances from a variety of guest performers on instruments and spoken word. The tone is one of focused calm (Newhere Music, October 2). A similar feeling is created by pianist Kris Davis, leading the Kris Davis Trio on Lost in Geneva, which sounds like being pleasantly found (4166, September 25). Spoken word meets musique concrète on the ambitious Chinese Benefits, recorded on a failing iPhone 6 by A Large Sheet of Muscle (Drowned by Locals, October 16). Pianist Kevin Hays is Live at the Stone. Each of the four pieces includes a guest appearance, which lends the set great tonal variety. One title is “Bob Dylan” (AHT, September 13). Jamie Safir‘s Momentism is playful and warm, a jazzy excursion from a quartet whose sound pairs well with the name of the label (Chill Tone, September 4). A Mind in Motion is the first of Shifting Paradigm‘s fall releases, guitarist Zebu Zheng in charge of a quartet, sounding personal and upbeat (September 18). Following in its wake is Andrew Toombs‘ Alloy; we love the blue and purple cover, along with the laidback grooves (October 16). And we’re not sure how long it takes to make a cake look like a circuit board, but if that’s a photograph on the cover of Twin Talk‘s Delights, color us impressed (October 13). Vibraphonist Jalen Baker leads a nonet on RePaved, a breezy collection of tunes that honors the history of Houston TX’s 3rd, 4th and 5th Wards (Cellar Music, September 4). Bassist Emma Dayhuff leads a septet on Mountains, which seeks to translate the wonder of Montanan vistas into jazz (Division 81, September 4). An eleven-piece ensemble performs A World That Bears a Question, a 28-part suite inspired by Haruki Murakami’s novel 1Q84. One need not read the novel to understand the music of Madre Vaca, but we recommend doing both at once (September 18). Contemporary jazz sextet ONMO offers In Time and Spirit, which draws from myriad influences and “sits outside of jazz time” (Clonmell Jazz Social, October 16). The self-titled album from Oslo ensemble Power Chords is hythmic and percussive, as captured in lead single “Clumsy,” an ironic title as “serendipitous” might make a better description (Sonic Transmissions, October 30). Moon Inhabitants invite you to experience Canned Luna, an exuberant explosion of Norwegian jazz. A sense of fun permeates the record, which has an infectious energy (Sauajazz, September 4). Also hailing from Norway, Hans P. Kjorstad finds room for jazz, folk, rock, modern composition and more in the welcoming Inn. An intriguing quirk of the “miniature orchestra” ~ each of the track titles has three letters (Phantom Limb, September 18).   Hypergarden‘s self-titled debut is a series of freeform jams bordering on rock. Our favorite title is “Invasion of the Hydrangeas” (September 25). The improvising trio Lothar Ohlmeier / Isambard Khroustaliov / Rudi Fischerlehner unveils Landscapes on October 9, referencing both musique concrète and punk (Not Applicable). Mike Reed’s Separatist Party is rocking and rolling on Sing the Color Blue, another left turn from the always reliable Thrill Jockey (October 22). Between avant jazz and noise lies the raucous Evangelium, from Frode Gjerstad / Karl Bjorå / Håvard Skaset. The music tumbles, intertwines and roars (Conradsound, October 1). Eyes of Moon is a loud, romping jam from Tomchess, a multi-instrumentalist joined by a cavalcade of stars (Amalgam, September 15). The iconoclastic Ka Baird teams with Chris Ryan Williams to present Enthalpy. Onomatopoeic vocals are laid atop diagonal instrumentation, sounding like curious creatures from another world (Outside Time, September 25). Richard Allen

items.body: Review by ianjferris@gmail.com — From my early teens in the early 1970's to this day, I'm a YES fan. All this last half century and more, it has been a marvellous band. Even their, sometimes musically dodgy, last four or five albums, up to and including their recent "Aurora", appeal to me. I like all of their stuff. Well nearly all - read on. I've got all their albums, most of them on both vinyl and CD (including ABWH), up to and including "Mirror to the Sky" (I downloaded "Aurora" from Apple Music as I don't have a physical copy yet on either cd or vinyl but I will have soon). One other exception - I don't (and never will) have a physical copy of "Heaven & Earth", which I have listened to several times digitally, on Apple Music. H&E is a truly awful release (on a par with that other truly awful release by another band, that most god-awful dirge "The Final Cut" by Pink Floyd). I also have fifteen live YES albums, including the "Live From Lyon" release with Benoit David on vocals! Great album. And now, having established my YES fan credentials, I come to my opinion on "Tales From Topographic Oceans". This will be short - hopefully no more than a dozen words (hence the long lead in, in order to pass the 100 word criteria)..... Overly long, self absorbed (read Jon A), pretentious (read Jon A), boring (there's a dozen words!). In my opinion, this is another "onion" in unison with Rick Wakeman's famous description of "Union". If "Tales....." had been more musically compact - one vinyl disc with 18 to 20 minutes of music on each side, - it could have been a great companion to "The YES Album" and "Fragile" and "Close to The Edge". It could have been the next progressive stage in the work of this band. As it turned out, it wasn't a progression. Nor was it a sideways move. It wasn't even a regression. The truth is that it wasn't (still isn't) anything except boring, pretentious (read Jon A), self absorbed (read Jon A) and overly long.One star.

items.body: Review by yarstruly — Clicking 5 but really 4.5, 4 is too low!Simultaneously posted to my blog (Scott's Song by Song Spotlights), with additional links and information.PsychoYogi are a UK prog band formed in 2010 and led by guitarist/vocalist/composer Chris Ramsing. The line up has evolved since their 2011 debut but has stabilized over the last few releases. Chris recently reached out to me to review the band's latest album "A World of Danger", released on November 28, 2025. As with my previous review, while it is not brand new or pre-release, it is certainly not an "old" album. This is their tenth studio album. According to Chris: "There is no theme, the main thing that connects the tunes is the downfall of mankind in the 21st century, each song has its own story?"As always, I receive no additional compensation other than the review copy of the album, and I always call it like I hear it. This is a cold listen.The line up for the album is:- Chris Ramsing / guitar, vocal- Izzy Stylish / bass- Tim Smart / trombone- Ben Woodbine-Craft / violin- Justin Casey / drums(How many prog bands sport a full-time trombonist? I would suspect there are few others, if any!)Track 1 - World of Danger (5:55)Jumping right in with the title track. It begins with a cool jazzy rhythm, and Tim Smart's trombone is prominent from the get-go. This has a very cool groove. The vocals could come out a little more but still sounds good. Chris has a reverse-recorded guitar solo at around the 2-minute mark. Loving the vibe of this. The arrangement is very creative. Izzy and Justin are a very talented rhythm section. The feeling is slightly sinister, like a film noir gangster. This really lives up to its title and sets the stage for a world of danger. Track 2 - Sometimes (2:49)This stays jazzy, but with a different groove. Lots of timing changes. I like Justin's cymbal work; not to mention the guiro and other assorted percussion novelties. The overall effect is slightly disorienting and implies a bit of a break with sanity. The closing verse kind of sums it up: In the asylum we're safe for a while and there's no expectations of who we should be, time doesn't matter and words have no meaning and less information is key.Another very cool track, albeit a short one!Track 3 - Blue in Rap City (3:05)The title is certainly a play on George Greshwin's "Rhapsody in Blue". The jazzy vibes continue, this time in a "joyfully strutting down the street" kind of way. This is such a unique sounding band! This one has a bit of a swing to it, but some odd meters keep you guessing. Izzy is walking all over the bass! Chris plays some classic jazz solos along the way. Tim Smart's trombone is very prominent. Ben Woodbine-Craft's violin, thus far, hasn't stood out, but has contributed in an ensemble serving fashion. Another fun, unique track!Track 4 - Mutual Agenda (2:59)The bass and drums play a few short rhythmic phrases, then, right on cue, the band kicks in and Ben is featured on violin. I promise this is a cold listen, typed in real time as I play each track. The contrasts between the instrumental segments are very interesting. The instrumental phrases are like a big band jazz thing, but the verses have vocals with guitar with a chorus effect on it. Another track that is unlike anything I have ever heard! (That's a good thing.)Track 5 - The Strangest Places (3:01)An air of mystery and Eastern flavor surrounds this one. Again, I'd like the vocals to be more out front. This feels like a snake-charmer dance. Super-cool! These guys are very talented! I like it! Just wish it were longer!Track 6 - Do That Dance (2:26)As we might expect, the jazziness continues. This one is a bit "sultry". The lyrics deal with individualism, and not falling in line with the crowd:I don't want to do that dance, smoke that thing or wear those pants, Parties make me feel remote, help me find the antidote.I don't want to pierce my nose, shave my head or decompose, fake a smile to win romance, I don't want to do that dance.A quick, fun little track.Track 7 - Moron (2:56)This has a tom-tom, smoky night club from back in the day, kind of a vibe. Very quirky! Middle Eastern style melodies help flavor the sound. Another cool, but short, jazzy track.Track 8 - For the Future (4:30)Belly-dance vibes abound! Very syncopated rhythms and odd meters are a big part of this. I like the unison instrumental phrases that are as tight as can be. This one makes me bob my head as I'm listening and typing. I like the vocal layering in the closing vocal section. The instruments take over to close it out. Cool tune!Track 9 - In Sight of the Goal (4:15)This one is also very syncopated, but not as bouncy as its predecessor. Much of it is in a meter of 7. Their arrangements are all so uniquely "them". Good track, but maybe not the strongest track on the album.Track 10 - Wonder Why (3:52)This one is a little bluesy; yet proggy too. Chris has such a nice, clean guitar tone. The trombone is what really gives the band their flavor. The final verse really asks a profound question:There's something troubling me, I can't begin to see,why children starve to please the rich,I'm sure you all agree and what will be will be.Kind of the state of the world right now.OVERALL IMPRESSIONS:This album goes to show that progressive isn't always defined by long tracks and head-spinning technically difficult phrases. That should not imply that this isn't a very talented band; they indeed are quite talented. This was a very difficult album for me, not in the sense of not liking it?I liked it a lot?but rather in the sense of having references jump into my mind for points of comparison. While I was aware of PsychoYogi prior to hearing this album, I hadn't heard very much until now. That is a situation that I intend to rectify, as I have added every available album to my streaming library. They don't sound like anyone that I am familiar with. And that is no easy task with there being so much music out there to listen to under the prog umbrella. Overall, I give this a 4.5 out of 5 (90%). If you already know PsychoYogi, then you already know it's unique. If, like me before listening to this album, you don't know them, I would highly recommend checking them out. If their earlier albums are anything like this one, they have carved out a unique niche in our prog world.

For me, betcover!!'s UMA is easily one of the most interesting, downright fun and genuinelystrange records to come out of Japan in recent years. Trying to put a label on it feels prettypointless, if I had to describe it it's simply jazz-rock with no limits.The first thing that grabbed me was the emotional range across the tracklist. In one song you feellike you're losing your mind to frantic rhythms, loud brass and wild energy. Then unexpectedly thenoise drops away, and you hear this quiet, deeply sad melody that cuts straight to the heart. Veryfew bands can pull off that kind of contrast without sounding messy or broken.Importantly, none of the intricate parts feel like showing off for the sake of it. The jazz turns,the prog patterns and the odd experiments blend together so naturally that the music always feelsalive and unpredictable, never sterile.It packs intense energy, complex ideas and deep sadness all into a single spin. That balance isessentially why I love both prog and jazz in the first place. It's not about cold technicalperfection, but the thrill of unpredictability and the actual emotional weight behind every note.Also, do yourself a favor and check out their live performances if you get the chance. The songstake on a completely different life on stage and the raw energy makes the whole thing hit evenharder.

items.body: Review by Kayhan — Messa's Close has completely stuck with me lately. It's definitely one of the freshest things I'veheard in the genre, mostly because hearing a doom metal band fold Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, andNorth African motifs into their sound without turning it into a cheap gimmick is pretty rare. Theybalance the thick, crushed doom riffs with loose stoner vibes really well, never losing that moodyatmosphere.The jazz phrasing and soulful guitar work give the record a lot of personality, especially whenpaired with traditional acoustic instruments like the oud. The tracklist takes a couple of sharpdetours, too. You get "Hollow," which is this quiet, eerie acoustic breather, and then right aroundthe corner is "Leffotrak"?a 45-second blast of raw, screamed aggression. On paper, it shouldn'twork, but it never actually breaks the album's flow.The real anchor here, though, is Sara Bianchin. Her voice is remarkably clean and subtle, avoidingany over-the-top dramatics, but it carries a quiet emotional weight that pulls you right into thetracks.Trackwise, "Pilgrim" is easily the highlight for me especially that acoustic build that detonatesinto a wall of heavy riffs. "Rubedo" has a killer solo, while "Serving Him" and "If You Want Her toBe Taken" hold up just as well. Solid, weird, and deeply rewarding listen from front to back.

items.body: Review by VianaProghead — Review N� 985"The Ten Legendary Singles" is a compilation of Led Zeppelin and was released in 1989. As the title suggests, it compiles the ten first and most successful singles released by the group on their entire career, including its respective B sides. It has songs from all their eighth studio albums plus a song that was only released on the compilation "Coda"."The Ten Legendary Singles" is a package with an easy to open box set with picture sleeves, a book focusing on the singles released and with a cover with a substantial painting. It was released with a very limited distribution before being discontinued. So, there's a good reason that very few have ever heard of this release and few have a copy of it."The Ten Legendary Singles" has twenty tracks. "Good Times Bad Times" and "Communication Breakdown" are from "Led Zeppelin". "Good Times Bad Times" is the A side and "Communication Breakdown" is the B side. "Good Times Bad Times" is a powerful rock song with nice riffs and a great vocal work with excellent chorus. "Communication Breakdown" is a powerful rock song with a great guitar riff. "Living Loving Maid (She's Just A Woman)" and "Whole Lotta Love" are from "Led Zeppelin II". "Whole Lotta Love" is the A side and "Living Loving Maid (She's Just A Woman)" is the B side. "Living Loving Maid (She's Just A Woman)" is a short catchy song with a nice guitar riff and a good vocal work. "Whole Lotta Love" is a song basically driven by a simple and typical but effective guitar riff of Page. "Immigrant Song" is from "Led Zeppelin III" and "Hey, Hey, What Can I Do" is a non-album's song. It was recorded, as a bonus track, on "Coda". "Immigrant Song" is the A side and "Hey, Hey, What Can I Do" is the B side. "Immigrant Song" is a very short track with a very fast tempo beat. "Hey Hey, What Can I Do" is an acoustic nice ballad, a bluesy rock piece. It's not great but it's not bad either. "Black Dog Man" and "Misty Mountain Hope" are from "Led Zeppelin IV". "Black Dog Man" is the A side and "Misty Mountain Hope" is the B side. "Black Dog" is a great and powerful song with a blues/rock riff and where Plant has one of his best vocal performances. "Misty Mountain Hop" is a great song that represents a good rock moment but isn't as good as most of the songs on that album. "Rock And Roll" and "Four Sticks" are from "Led Zeppelin IV" too. "Rock And Roll" is the A side and "Four Sticks" is the B side. "Rock And Roll" is a fantastic straight typical Rock'n'Roll number with a great drumming work and a nice guitar work. "Four Sticks", like "Misty Mountain Hop", is also a great song, but hasn't the same quality level of the most of the songs on that album. "Over The Hills And Far Away" and "Dancing Days" are from "Houses Of The Holy". "Over The Hills And Far Away" is the A side and "Dancing Days" is the B side. "Over The Hills And Far Away" has a great acoustic guitar performance by Page. It's an interesting song that mixes the beautiful acoustic ballad with the hard rock. "Dancing Days" is one of the most commercial songs on that album. It's good, but less good than some of the songs on that album. "The Crunge" and "D'yer Ma'ker" are from "Houses Of The Holy" too. "D'yer Ma'ker" is the A side and "The Crunge" is the B side. "The Crunge" is a funky song, a tribute to James Brown. I never liked particularly of this song really. "D'yer Mak'er" is a song influenced by reggae. It isn't a bad song but it's out of the context of that album. "Trampled Under Foot" and "Black Country Woman" are from "Physical Graffiti". "Trampled Under Foot" is the A side and "Black Country Woman" is the B side. "Trampled Under Foot" is a kind of catchy song with relatively complex arrangements especially on Page's guitar effects and riffs. "Black Country Woman" is an acoustic blues 517song. It's a typical folk song with good vocals and pounding drumming. "Royal Orleans" and "Candy Store Rock" are from "Presence". "Candy Store Rock" is the A side and "Royal Orleans" is the B side. "Royal Orleans" is a funky influenced song with a nice drumming performance on it. "Candy Store Rock" is a monotonous boring song. Like "Royal Orleans", it's a weak song for Led Zeppelin. "Fool In The Rain" and "Hot Dog" are from "In Through The Out Door". "Fool In The Rain" is the A side and "Hot Dog" is the B side. "Fool In The Rain" is a song dominated by piano with a Latin touch. It spans several genres with a surprising samba section. "Hot Dog" is influenced by country music. I don't like particularly of this kind of music.Conclusion: "The Ten Legendary Singles" is a strange and special compilation album from Led Zeppelin. For those, like me, who have all the ten studio albums from the band, we may say this is probably an item with little interest. In reality, it has only one track that we can't get on their official studio discography, "Hey, Hey, What Can I Do". So, we can ask, who is interested in a compilation like this? In my humble opinion, there's only one kind of person that can be hardly interested in it, the most diehard fans of the band. I've no doubt in saying this is a real blessing for those who can purchase a rare gem like this. Still, despite the good quality, I'm sure this isn't a great item that is worth hunting, especially because it's a very fairly impracticable purchase and very expensive to get it, if that's possible. So, according to what I said before, "The Ten Legendary Singles" is a good addition, but only to any collector fan of Led Zeppelin.Prog is my Ferrari. Jem Godfrey (Frost*)

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — There are very special live albums that, despite not featuring new studio material, innovate through their arrangements or live performances. This gives them a unique quality, one just as valuable as that of conventional studio productions.Renaissance's live album at Carnegie Hall is special for many reasons. No other band integrated an orchestra into its compositional and performance dynamics quite like Renaissance; indeed, the New York Philharmonic acts as an additional member of the group. The performances by John Tout on piano and Jon Camp on bass are superb, particularly because they improvise and venture beyond the familiar versions of the songs (the true hallmark of a great live album, and what gives it a life of its own). And finally, there is Annie Haslam, the star and heart of the group, whose voice (exquisite and pristine) guided both band and audience safely home, much like the sirens' song to Ulysses, though in this instance, leading them in the right direction."Prologue", which was on the first album featuring Annie in the band, was always one of my favorite tracks: its opening, evoking Chopin's "Revolutionary" Etude, followed by that jazz-style fugue. Annie doesn't sing; instead, she follows the melody with her voice, and nothing more is needed. "Can You Understand" is another track that packs a punch live; the piano and bass exude confidence, and when the clavinet joins in, a whole new dimension comes into play. The song is from Ashes Are Burning, another of the band's classic albums. Here, the clavinet sounds deeper and more pronounced, making the gateway to another realm, into which the quintet always transports us, feel all the more immediate. The orchestra is also present, and the moments with an Oriental flavor sound enigmatic and emotionally dark, more so than ever before."Running Hard" is from one of my favorite albums, Turn of the Cards, actually the first one I ever Heard, and its piano introduction sounds just as breathtaking live as the original; it embodies not only Romanticism but also Impressionism. The introduction to "Mother Russia" is also noticeably different from the familiar version, featuring a very delicate piano section, followed by a passage enhanced by the power of the live orchestra.Jon Camp shares a bit of the history of "Song of Scheherazade" with the audience before the performance begins; the bass work shines, and the orchestra truly comes into its own, weaving together Arabian and Eastern motifs with Spaghetti Western elements reminiscent of Ennio Morricone. The choir rivals the power of Pink Floyd's Atom Heart Mother in its grandeur and sonic impact. The vocal sections and central melody are every bit as perfect and wonderful as the familiar ones, and the voices of Annie and Jon blend ideally in their duet. The orchestra's trombones and horns seem to float in the air as Annie's voice soars even higher... and what is there to say? Every time you hear it, it feels like the very first time."Ashes Are Burning" expands from eleven minutes to nearly twenty-four, featuring new improvisational sections where the bass, drums, and piano trio truly shine. Once again, the clavinet is brought prominently to the fore, followed by a jazz-infused section with impeccable timing and a passionate bass solo that maintains the tension throughout, creating the feeling of actually being there with the band.The album was released at a pivotal momento, 1976, crowning the band's golden era, during which they pushed the possibilities of the very style they had created to the limit. I am sure the performance benefited because the band fed off the audience's energy, that unique communion that can only happen at live shows.

items.body: Jamaican singer and songwriter Protoje filmed part of the video for “1000 Lashes” inside the Adwa Victory Memorial Museum in Addis Ababa, built on the site where Ethiopian forces defeated invading Italian troops in 1896 and kept the country free of colonial rule. Born in Saint Elizabeth and twice nominated for the Best Reggae Album Grammy for A Matter of Time and Third Time’s the Charm, the artist confronts the moral cost of global inequality before turning that inquiry onto his own life. Writing from a position of relative privilege, he weighs his own domestic comfort through the line “I’ve got my blessings and I’m feeling no pain,” before reflecting on generational injustice, exploitation, and child labour once his front door closes. Guest vocalist Stephen Marley sings the chorus, “All the children are ours,” right after Protoje admits his own peace. The next verse lists what that peace costs elsewhere: backs lashed a thousand times, communities broken apart, opportunities stolen, wrongdoing shielded by immunity, and children working mines and sent into conflict. SAMO directed the video across two sites bound up in that history: the museum in Addis Ababa, and the steps of 56 Hope Road in Kingston, the Marley family home turned museum. “1000 Lashes” is extracted from The Art of Acceptance, Protoje’s latest album arrived in April via In.Digg.Nation Collective and Ineffable Records. He plays Ruhr Reggae Summer in Mülheim an der Ruhr and Uprising Festival in Bratislava across the same weekend at the end of August, followed by dates across the United States through September and the Welcome to Jamrock Reggae Cruise in November. items.body: Berlin darkwave and synthpop band Blutengel released the single and video “Afterlife” on 4 September 2026 via Out Of Line Music. The track is the third single from Blutengel’s upcoming studio album, due in early 2027, following “The Devil” in October 2025 and “Schwarzer Engel” in June 2026. “Afterlife” is a slow-building darkwave track built on melancholic, cinematic electronics carried by a steady pulse. The song combines layered synthesizer parts with a melodic hook, moving between an introspective verse structure and a club-ready tempo. The single arrives ahead of Blutengel’s headline appearance at Dark Summer Open Air Vol. 2, at Wasserschloss Klaffenbach in Chemnitz, on 12 September 2026, with Chrom, Destroy Me Again and Ghostbells confirmed as support. Out Of Line Music describes the show as nearing a sellout. About Blutengel Blutengel was formed in Berlin in 1998 by singer Chris Pohl after he left Seelenkrank, and released its debut album, “Child of Glass,” in 1999. Ulrike Goldmann joined as co-vocalist in 2005 and remains in the band alongside Pohl. Blutengel has released its albums through Out Of Line Music, building a chart record in Germany that includes “Monument” (No. 4, 2013), “Omen” (No. 4, 2015), “Leitbild” (No. 4, 2017), “Un:Gott” (No. 2, 2019) and “Erlösung – The Victory of Light” (No. 4, 2021). Its most recent studio album, “Dämonen: Sturm,” was released in February 2025. Blutengel has since issued “The Devil,” “Schwarzer Engel” and now “Afterlife” as singles ahead of a new studio album planned for early 2027.
